name: Southeast Slopes / Standard Scramble
findings: Trailhead pin is the Rainy Pass PCT lot; the itinerary now starts at the SR-20 turnout 3.1 mi east.

row.name: Southeast Slopes / Standard Scramble
hazards: Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies during spring snow season
Loose talus, scree, and some loose rock in the summit gullies
Seasonal waterfall/creek crossing at the base of the west gully descent line
Afternoon thunderstorms common on the exposed ridge in summer
No reliable cell coverage in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor
row.overview: A non-technical summit on the Okanogan Range crest between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass, in Chelan County within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. Whistler is linked by a high ridge to Cutthroat Peak (8,050 ft), 0.8 mile north-northeast, and offers a broad, mostly-talus scramble popular as an early-season warm-up or a corn-snow ski descent in late spring. The standard route climbs the mountain's south ridge and southwest slope; a steeper alternative ascends a broad gully system visible from Rainy Pass.
row.beta: From a roadside turnout on SR-20 (or alternatively the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead), a boot path climbs through open forest and a meadow basin, then rises on a traversing line to intersect the level part of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there the route follows the ridge and adjoining gullies — staying north of a loose gully band and using a visible ramp near the headwall — to the 7,790 ft summit; an alternative continues the ridge to about 6,800 ft before cutting left across gullies onto gentler terrain on the southwest slope for the final push. It is class 3 scrambling throughout, with class 4 moves possible depending on line choice.
row.turnaround: In spring/early summer when the gullies still hold snow, turn around by late morning to avoid wet-slab avalanche release as the sun softens the snowpack; on the dry-season south-ridge route, the main time pressure is afternoon thunderstorm buildup over the crest.
row.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent route down the south ridge / southwest slope.
obj_haz: Cornices along the upper ridge and gully rims in winter/spring
Wet, heavy maritime snow prone to wet-slab avalanches

waypoints.name: Meadow rising traverse
waypoints.note: Boot path climbs through an open meadow then angles into a rising traverse aiming for the crest of Whistler's south ridge; faint tread, easy to lose in fog.

waypoints.name: South ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Boot path tops out on the level section of Whistler's south ridge here; from this point the route follows the ridge and connecting gullies toward the summit.

waypoints.name: 6,800 ft ridge/gully split
waypoints.note: Ridge steepens; here parties can cut left across gullies onto the gentler southwest slope as an easier alternative to staying directly on the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Summit ridge scramble band
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 terrain mixes downsloping slabs and loose gravel on ledges just below the summit ridge; a helmet is worth carrying for rockfall and slip potential here.

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass Trailhead (PCT North parking lot, SR-20)

sectionBreakdown.note: A single-day round trip from the SR-20 turnout east of Rainy Pass (about 5,000 ft): climb through a meadow to gain the south ridge around 6,180 ft, then follow rock and gully terra…

row.detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble route; parties typically carry trekking poles for the meadow/traverse sections, a helmet for the loose ridge and gully terrain, and an ice axe (with willingness to turn back if conditions warrant crampons) when snow lingers in the gullies in early season.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and traction (crampons/microspikes) for snow-covered gullies in spring/early summer
Layers for an exposed, wind-prone ridge
pro_tips: The Rainy Pass PCT-lot gully approach doubles as a well-regarded spring corn-snow ski descent — go early enough to catch the snow softening but before it turns to mush
On the south-ridge route, cutting left across gullies at ~6,800 ft onto the southwest slope avoids the harder gully scrambling higher on the ridge crest
watch_out: Trailhead access disappears entirely once SR 20's winter gates close (roughly late Nov–late Apr/mid-May) — check WSDOT pass status first
The unmarked highway pullout for the south-ridge route is easy to miss; it's 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass and 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead
Early-season (May-June) ascents will find the gullies holding consolidated snow — carry an ice axe and know how to self-arrest
The west-gully descent funnels toward a seasonal waterfall — exit right into the glades to avoid it
row.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no fixed protection or technical rack; a rope and basic protection could be carried by conservative parties for the class 4 variations, but are not standard.
row.approach: Two trailheads serve the Southeast Slopes / South Ridge scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.
row.descent_text: There is no rappelling on the standard Southeast Slopes/South Ridge route — it's a walk-off/downclimb, reversing whichever line was used on the way up. From the summit, downclimb the summit gully (loose gravel and downsloping slabs — take care with rockfall for anyone below) back to the shoulder, then descend either the west ridge/gully back into the meadow basin and forest (Option A) or drop onto the south ridge and retrace the rising traverse back to the meadow and boot path to the highway turnout (Option B). Loose rock and talus in the gullies is the main descent hazard — down-climb facing in on the steeper class 3 sections and stay alert for parties below. Some ski mountaineers descend a separate snow-filled west gully (~35°, over 1,000 ft of sustained fall-line terrain funneling to a waterfall lower down, requiring an exit right into the glades to avoid the falls) as a spring ski descent, but that is a snow-season variant, not part of the standard summer scramble descent, and should not be used as a hiking descent once snow is out. rappels: 0.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward by reversing the scramble at any point; no committing technical sections.

pitch_detail.notes: Boot path from the SR-20 turnout, leaving from the west edge of a stand of trees and climbing up through a meadow.
Rising traverse across the meadow/talus to intersect the level part of the south ridge at 6,180 ft.

Follow the ridge and adjoining gullies to the 7,790 ft summit, staying north of the loosest gully band and using a visible ramp to bypass rock near the headwall; an alternative cuts left at ~6,800 ft onto gentler southwest-slope terrain.

itinerary.cal: Snow often lingers in the summit gullies into early-mid summer; best conditions are typically July-September once SR-20 (Rainy Pass) has been open a while and gullies have melted out.

days.note: A single-day round trip from the SR-20 turnout east of Rainy Pass (about 5,000 ft): climb through a meadow to gain the south ridge around 6,180 ft, then follow rock and gully terrain (class 3-4) to the 7,790 ft summit before reversing the same line back to the car. No camping is involved — this is done entirely car-to-car.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble

schedule.label: Leave the SR-20 turnout
schedule.detail: Park at the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (~5,000 ft), walk back along the shoulder and pick up the boot path at the west edge of a stand of trees.

schedule.detail: Rising traverse through meadow to intersect the level part of the south ridge near 6,180 ft.

days.objective: Summit Whistler Mountain via the South Ridge and return to the highway turnout

itinerary.totalNote: A moderate single-day scramble: about 4 miles round trip with 3,000 ft of gain, typically 6-8 hours car-to-car from the highway turnout; no overnight component.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day at the Rainy Pass trailhead (cash/check or digital day pass); Northwest Forest Pass and Interagency (America the Beautiful) passes also honored.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambling.
access.closures: Entire approach is inaccessible whenever SR 20 is under its winter closure (roughly late Nov through late Apr/mid-May); confirm current road status with WSDOT before driving in.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Winthrop, WA)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or $5 day-use fee at Rainy Pass trailhead

overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass, an America the Beautiful pass, or a Recreation.gov day pass covers parking at the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead; no permit paperwork is needed to camp anywhere along this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR 20)
road.status: Paved highway, open only when seasonal snow gates are up
road.driveNote: Drive SR 20 over Rainy Pass; the two trailhead options (Rainy Pass PCT lot, or the unmarked pullout 3.1 mi east of the pass) are both directly off the highway with no additional dirt-road driving.
road.seasonalGate: Gated closed for winter — gates at Diablo (west) and Early Winters near Mazama (east). Typically closes late November and reopens late April to mid-May depending on snowpack; check WSDOT's pass report before planning a trip.

climate.fall: Cools quickly with possible early-season snow at elevation; SR-20 access can end abruptly with the season's first significant highway closure.
climate.spring: Snowpack still substantial into May/June on north- and gully-facing terrain; the west-facing gully is a documented corn-snow ski descent in late May.
climate.summer: Generally dry with occasional afternoon thunderstorms typical of the eastern Cascades crest; the standard scramble window.
climate.winter: SR-20 gated/closed through the Washington Pass-Rainy Pass corridor; the peak is inaccessible by the standard trailhead.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with a strong maritime influence even on this east-slope Cascades peak; winter and spring snow tends to be wet and heavy, producing high avalanche danger on the gullied approaches. Summers are typically dry with mostly clear skies, though afternoon thunderstorms can build over the Cascade crest.

bySeason.fall: Good scrambling into September/early October; watch for early-season snow and shortening daylight.
bySeason.spring: Deep, often unstable wet snow fills the gullies (used for ski descents); avalanche and cornice hazard is significant — check NWAC before going.
bySeason.summer: Typical dry-scramble season once snow clears the upper slopes, usually by mid-to-late July; talus and scree underfoot.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent in the Rainy Pass/Washington Pass corridor; the nearest reliable help is the highway itself — flag down traffic or drive to Mazama/Winthrop. This stretch of SR 20 is remote and, once winter gates close, entirely inaccessible.
emergency.county: Chelan County (summit); the SR 20 approach corridor runs along the Chelan/Okanogan county line near Rainy and Washington Passes
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA, (509) 996-4000
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA — 24-hour ER, (509) 689-2517
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Okanogan County Sheriff (trailhead/highway side) — for backcountry incidents, contact via 911; confirm jurisdiction may hand off to Chelan County SAR depending on exact location

crowds.peakTraffic: weekends July-September; the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead itself sees heavy thru-hiker and day-hiker traffic, but most of that traffic splits off and does not continue up toward Whistler's summit gully
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 20-50 parties per season (estimate) - a known but secondary North Cascades scramble objective, well behind trade routes like Mailbox Peak or Colchuck

fitnessSpec.hiking: Able to sustain ~4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft of gain at elevation (trailhead near 4,850 ft, summit 7,790 ft), typically a 6-9 hour round trip
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (10-20 lb) - water, layers, helmet; no technical rack needed in normal summer conditions

partner_requirements.approachTime: 2-3 hours from the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead to the base of the summit gully, then additional time for the talus scramble to the top
requiredSkills: basic navigation off-trail once leaving the PCT
self-arrest/step-kicking awareness for lingering early-season snow patches
afternoon-thunderstorm judgment (turnaround discipline on an exposed summit)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Comfortable, unroped Class 3 scrambler; should have prior experience on loose talus/scree and basic alpine routefinding, since the route is a gully/slope scramble rather than a maintained trail to the top

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early October, once snow has melted off the upper slopes

July.reason: Snow typically clears from the upper gully by mid-July; long daylight and stable summer weather, though early-July ascents can still hit lingering snowfields

August.reason: Most reliable month - talus fully exposed, driest conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are common and should be watched for

October.reason: Early season snow can return to the high pass terrain at any time, days are short, and North Cascades Highway/access conditions become less predictable

September.reason: Still generally dry and clear with fewer bugs and crowds than midsummer, but shorter daylight and first frosts begin

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades crest weather at ~7,800 ft: cool mornings, warm midday, and rapid weather swings; the Washington Pass area is prone to sudden cloud buildup even on otherwise clear forecasts
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August - plan for an early start and to be off the summit before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low-to-moderate: Class 2-3 scrambling terrain, but the loose talus and scree footing creates real twisted-ankle and rockfall-onto-partner risk, especially in the gully where parties stack above one another; lingering early-summer snowfields can add a slip hazard on the approach gully before full melt-out

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; NWAC does not issue forecasts for this zone/period since the route is climbed outside the Nov-May avalanche season

gaps: No confirmed first-ascent date or party found
Exact county boundary (Chelan vs. Okanogan) at the summit itself not independently confirmed beyond Wikipedia
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the PCT North trailhead parking at Rainy Pass on SR-20 (~4,860 ft)

row.rope_note: Non-technical: boot path from SR-20 near Rainy Pass up through meadows to the south ridge (6180ft), then ridge/gully scrambling to the summit. No roped climbing required.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

climbing_route.label: Col to the summit shoulder via the west ridge (Option A)
climbing_route.notes: From the meadow basin at about 6,100 ft trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder. Trail-less with route-finding and loose talus/scree in the gullies, and real exposure near the ridge crest; early-season snow can make the gully sections firm or icy.

climbing_route.label: Final rock gully and headwall ramp
climbing_route.notes: The final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above.

climbing_route.label: South ridge from 6,180 ft (Option B)
climbing_route.notes: Intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft, then scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; loose talus/scree in the gullies and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully.

climbing_route.label: Southwest slopes variant
climbing_route.notes: Alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

name: Iceman
findings: Ice Box: road/trailhead pin says Cutthroat/Blue Lake, not the SR-20 hairpin; approach text describes the Alpenkuhl crag.

row.name: Iceman
row.season: Summer — a shaded destination good for hot days when nearby Mazama crags are too warm.
hazards: Slick approach slabs pose a fall hazard on the hike in, independent of the climbing itself.
Alpine granite setting means occasional loose rock off-route.
row.overview: A one-pitch 5.10a/b line up the shaded Ice Box (Left Side) buttress, the 'dead middle' finger-crack/roof line splitting sport routes Route C and Route D.
row.beta: Climbs a steep face on good holds to a bolt guarding a thin finger-crack move, then finishes on horizontal cracks into an awkward but enjoyable left-facing corner. Mixed protection (3 bolts plus small-to-mid cams) makes it the trad line of the three Ice Box routes.
row.turnaround: Start early enough to be off the exposed approach slabs and rock before afternoon thunderstorms, which are common in the North Cascades in summer; treat the slick granite slabs as more hazardous in rain.
row.face: Ice Box (left side), Hairpin Crags — the finger-crack line between two of the sport routes
row.comms: No cell phone service is available at Washington Pass or along this stretch of the North Cascades Highway corridor per NPS and WSDOT; do not rely on a signal for emergencies.
row.descent: Lower or rappel from the anchor back to the base.
obj_haz: Smooth, slippery approach slabs above the dry creek bed (fall hazard, worse when wet)
Loose rock possible on unfeatured alpine granite

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Same trailhead used for the Concord/Lexington cluster; from the climber's path, cut right into a dry creek bed and ascend fixed-line slabs to the Ice Box.

waypoints.name: Ice Box Left Side Base
waypoints.note: Base of the Ice Box wall, shared by Iceman, Route C, and Route D; approach slabs are smooth and slippery.

row.detailed_rack: 3 fixed bolts protect the crux face and finger-crack section; supplement with a small rack of cams from about BD #0.3 to #1 for the horizontal-crack and corner finish. A single 60m rope and standard quickdraws/alpine draws are sufficient for this one-pitch route.
what_to_bring: Approach shoes suited to slick granite slabs
pro_tips: Good handholds on the initial face make the opening moves easier than they look — save gear placements for after the bolt-protected finger-crack crux.
Combine with neighboring Route C and Route D for a full day at this shaded, cooler crag.
row.watch_out:
Approach slabs above the dry creek bed are smooth and slippery, and the lower slab has no hand-line — worse when wet.
Only the crux face and finger crack are bolted; the horizontal cracks and left-facing corner above need your own small-to-mid cams.
Alpine granite can shed occasional loose rock off-route.
row.pro_needs: Mixed protection — 3 bolts plus a handful of small-to-medium cams (0.3-1 BD equivalent) placed in the horizontal cracks and finishing corner.
row.best_season: Late June through September, matching the broader Washington Pass climbing season; the Ice Box's shaded, north-facing character keeps it cooler than sunnier Washington Pass walls and can hold wet rock or residual snow later into the early season.
row.approach: Spire Gully right (Alpenkuhl), part of the Hairpin Crags, is reached from the same large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 near Washington Pass used for Kangaroo Temple. Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall). The approach is one of the shortest at Washington Pass — a direct walk/scramble of roughly 10-15 minutes straight up from the highway, snow-covered in early season and a worn boot path later in summer.
row.descent_text: From the top anchor, lower on a single strand or rappel with a 60m rope directly back to the base of the route; no walk-off is required for this single-pitch line.
row.bail: Straightforward retreat on a single-pitch route — lower or rappel off the highest gear/bolt placed at any point.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep face on good holds to a bolt protecting a thin finger-crack section, then horizontal cracks into a left-facing corner finish.

row.itinerary: A single-day cragging objective, typically combined with Route C and/or Route D at the same crag: drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20, approach via the slab/creek-bed trail, climb, then lower/rappel and retrace the approach to the car.

_raw.permit_type: Free self-issued wilderness permit for overnight stays
_raw.permit_pickup: Self-issued at trailhead or ranger stations
_raw.special_hazards: Smooth, slippery slabs; first slab without fixed line; approach requires scrambling

name: Church Lake Scramble
findings: Approach now says the trail passes the EAST side of the lake; waypoint[3] pin still sits west of the lake.

row.name: Church Lake Scramble
gear: sturdy hiking boots or approach shoes
ice axe (seasonal — snowpack lingers in the basin into July)
helmet (optional, for loose rock on the final ~100m scramble)
hazards: exposed class 3 ridge near the summit
heather and slab when wet
row.overview: Bearpaw Mountain (6,091 ft) is a short, steep scramble summit above Church Lake, just east of Church Mountain in the Nooksack Ridge high country north of Mount Baker. It's reached by an unmaintained boot path (not an official Forest Service trail) from the end of FS Road 3160, off Canyon Creek Road, climbing past Church Lake and up open ridge/meadow terrain to a narrow, sometimes-exposed class 3 finish.
row.beta: From the Church Lake trailhead at the end of FS Road 3160, an easy but steep unofficial path climbs about 0.6 miles to Church Lake. From the lake the route continues around the shore and up through meadows toward a ridge/saddle above, then follows the ridge — which becomes steep but is 'nothing scary' — to a high point near peak 6066, with the final ~100 meters to the true summit requiring some class 3 scrambling on a narrow, occasionally exposed ridge. This is a hiker/scrambler route, not a roped climb; no technical gear is used on it.
row.turnaround: Because the final ridge to the summit is narrow, loose, and exposed in places, turn around well before dusk and reassess if the ridge is wet, snow-covered, or if any party member is uncomfortable with unroped class 3 exposure — the terrain does not forgive a rushed or fatigued descent.
row.comms: Remote North Cascades terrain near the Canadian border with no cell coverage expected at the trailhead, Church Lake, or on the summit ridge; do not rely on a cell phone for emergency contact in this area.
row.descent: Reverse the ridge and boot path back down to Church Lake and the FS Road 3160 trailhead.
obj_haz: exposed, narrow ridge scramble near the summit

waypoints.name: FS Road 3160 End Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the rough, single-lane FS Road 3160 (high-clearance/4x4 recommended); unmaintained boot path to Church Lake starts here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Canyon Creek Road (FS-31) north off SR-542 just east of Glacier, then FS-3160 to its end at about 4,800 ft. The upper road is single-lane and rough, high clearance is the usual advice, and the parking is no more than a wide spot at the end.

waypoints.name: Boot Path Junction / Old Roadbed
waypoints.note: Unmarked user-built path leaves the old roadbed and climbs through brush toward the lake basin.
waypoints.directions: Continue on the old roadbed past the parking area for a couple of hundred yards. The user-built path toward the lake basin leaves it unmarked, though motorbike use has worn the line in well enough to follow.

waypoints.name: Church Lake
waypoints.note: Emerald subalpine lake in a basin below Bearpaw; established rough camp spots on the shore, often overgrown approach.
waypoints.directions: The path climbs steeply through forest — the steepest sustained grade of the day, about 400 ft — then rolls over a rise into the cirque holding the lake, 0.6 to 0.7 mile from the car.

waypoints.name: Left Rim of Church Lake Basin
waypoints.note: Keep left around the lake and start climbing the rim of the basin toward Point 6066 rather than following the lakeshore fully around.
waypoints.directions: Skirt the lake along its east/left shore rather than following the shoreline the whole way around, then start up the rim of the basin on the left (east) toward Point 6066. Fill water at the lake; there is none above it.

waypoints.name: Steep Heather/Meadow Ridge Below Point 6066
waypoints.note: Steep, loose tread through heather and meadow gains the ridge crest; described by hikers as steep but 'nothing scary' in dry conditions, slick when wet.
waypoints.directions: Above the lake the tread fades into intermittent boot path and cairns through meadow and heather benches, and the rim steepens on loose footing. Straightforward when dry, genuinely slick when wet, and snow lingers on the shaded slopes here into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Point 6066 Knoll
waypoints.note: Knoll with 270-degree views from Mount Baker eastward into Canada; the narrow summit ridge to Bearpaw's true top begins here.
waypoints.directions: Keep working up the rim to the broad high point on the ridge dividing Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block. This stretch accounts for most of the day's remaining gain.

waypoints.name: Exposed Summit Ridge
waypoints.note: Narrow, sometimes exposed ridgeline with loose footing for the final approach; use caution, easy to slip off either side.
waypoints.directions: From the knoll drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky, heathery bowl toward the base of the summit block, picking up the narrow connecting ridge. Footing is loose and the crest is exposed on both sides in places.

waypoints.name: Bearpaw Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; final ~100m from the ridge is a short Class 2-3 scramble over blocky rock.
waypoints.directions: The last stretch is a short Class 2-3 scramble, roughly 100 m, on generally solid blocky rock with mild exposure. Reverse the same ground to descend, or drop the scree-and-dirt chute that cuts straight from the ridge down to the lakeshore — quicker, but loose enough that it is no place to be below another party.

sectionBreakdown.note: A short, roadside scramble done entirely car-to-car in a half day. An easy, well-used boot path climbs steeply to Church Lake in well under an hour, then fainter tread continues up…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Church Lake to Bearpaw Mountain summit

row.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack applies to this route. It is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble — no cams, nuts, rope, or protection are used at any point, including the final steep section below the summit.
what_to_bring: trekking poles for the short, steep boot path to Church Lake
ice axe or microspikes if attempting in spring/early summer while snow persists in the cirque (reported to linger into July)
sturdy trail shoes or light hiking boots
navigation aid (map/GPS) since the climbers' path fades to a boot-track past Church Lake through the alpine meadows/cirque
sun protection for the open alpine basin
helmet if concerned about loose rock on the final scramble (optional, not reported as standard practice)
pro_tips: This is a short, steep half-day trip (~3.7 mi round trip, ~1,300 ft gain from the FS 3160 road end) — not a long remote approach
Check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF road status for Canyon Creek Road (FS 31) and spur FS 3160 before driving; this road has a history of slide closures
Helmet recommended for the loose rock and exposed ridge scrambling near the summit
watch_out: loose rock and route-finding on the unmaintained boot path
narrow, exposed class 3 ridge near the summit
lingering snowfields into early summer that can obscure the path
row.pro_needs: None. This is an unroped scramble; there are no protectable technical moves. The final ~100m to the summit is loose Class 2-3 terrain handled by careful route-finding and hand-and-foot scrambling, not by placing gear.
row.approach: From the FS 3160 road-end parking (roughly 48.957°N, 121.851°W, reached via Canyon Creek Road/FS 31 then FS 3160 as noted above), the route follows an unmaintained but well-worn boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail, just a heavily used user track — that climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft of gain to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake sitting in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first pitch is the steepest sustained grade of the day. Skirt the lake along its east/left shore (best flat campsites are on the far side, useful if splitting the trip). Beyond the lake the trail fades into intermittent boot-path and cairns through meadows and heather benches; keep left (east) up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block — this stretch accounts for most of the remaining ~900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 mi one-way (matching the ~5.9 km round trip). From the 6,066 ft knoll, drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky/heather bowl toward the base of Bearpaw's summit block; the final approximately 300 ft to the 6,091 ft summit is easy class 2-3 scrambling on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last pitch. Church Lake is the last reliable water source — carry water from there for the upper mountain. There is no maintained tread past the lake, so route-finding by cairns and boot-path is necessary, and in early/mid-season lingering snow on the steep initial slope above the lake and in the summit gullies can require an ice axe and caution; parties often find snow patches into July on shaded sections.
row.descent_text: Descend the same line: from the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 scramble terrain back to the 6,066 ft knoll above Church Lake basin. From there most parties either retrace the rim/boot-path back down into the basin, or drop via a direct scree/dirt gully (chute) that cuts straight down from the ridge to the lake's shore, shortcutting the traverse — this chute is loose underfoot (scree and dirt over rock) and warrants care with footing and any parties below; if snow lingers in the chute (common into early summer) an ice axe and basic self-arrest awareness are worthwhile. From Church Lake, retrace the 0.6-0.7 mile boot path back down to the FS 3160 trailhead. This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb scramble — no rope or rappelling is used on this route.
row.bail: Bail is short and simple — descend back to Church Lake and follow the boot path to the FS 3160 road end.

itinerary.cal: Road (FS 3160) and upper snow patches typically clear by mid-summer; best conditions are roughly July through September.

days.note: A short, roadside scramble done entirely car-to-car in a half day. An easy, well-used boot path climbs steeply to Church Lake in well under an hour, then fainter tread continues up rolling alpine meadows and a ridge toward Point 6066 before a final short class 2-3 scramble gains the true summit. Most parties are back at the trailhead by early-to-mid afternoon.

road.name: Canyon Creek Road (FS 31) to FS Road 3160
road.status: Open (high-clearance recommended); historically subject to slide damage and repair
road.driveNote: From Glacier, follow Canyon Creek Road (FS 31) to the first major fork, then FS Road 3160 to its end (~4.4 rough miles; high-clearance recommended). FS 31 has a recent history of slide closures beyond mile 4 — verify current road status before driving.
road.seasonalGate: Typically drivable/snow-free roughly June–October; check current MBS road conditions.

climate.fall: Cooling, wetter conditions from September on; hunting season begins August 1.
climate.spring: Persistent snow on the ridge and access road well into early summer; road may be snow-blocked.
climate.summer: Best window (roughly June/July-September) once trail and ridge are snow-free.
climate.winter: Heavy snow, road unmaintained/likely inaccessible, avalanche terrain on approach slopes.
climate.typical: Maritime border-country weather; snow lingers late at elevation.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate all-day hiking fitness for a short, steep ~3.7 mi round-trip day scramble with about 1,300 ft of gain — not the long remote approach the previous text implied.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Day-pack only; this is a car-to-car outing, not an overnight trip.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Short - the boot path reaches Church Lake in well under an hour, and the whole route is typically a 4-5 hour, ~3.7 mi round-trip car-to-car day trip.
requiredSkills: Off-trail route-finding and navigation on a fading, unmaintained boot path/cairned route above Church Lake
Comfortable on Class 2-3 rock and heather slopes, including short exposed steps near the summit
Judgment for lingering snow patches at elevation early in the season
Basic self-sufficiency, since help is not immediately at hand despite the short approach
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler comfortable with off-trail route-finding and short Class 2-3 exposure; a good short day-trip objective, not a remote/overnight undertaking

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-August through September, once the high country has melted out

July.reason: Snow lingers late at this elevation; route-finding and footing are harder, and some slopes may still be snow-covered

June.reason: Deep snow still covers approach slopes and the summit scramble; not in season

August.reason: Scramble season is established once high country has melted; best combination of dry rock/heather and stable weather

October.reason: Border-country weather deteriorates and early snow can return, closing the short seasonal window

September.reason: Continuation of the short clear scramble window before fall weather moves in

weather.typical: Maritime border-country weather with snow lingering late at elevation; conditions can be colder and wetter than lower-elevation Cascades due to proximity to the Canadian border
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving weather are possible in late summer; limited visibility on off-trail terrain compounds route-finding difficulty if weather closes in

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate fall exposure on Class 2-3 rock steps and heather slopes that become slick when wet; the remote, isolated setting significantly raises the consequence of any injury given the long evacuation distance

avalanche.zone: NWAC Mt Baker zone covers the broader area, but no zone is published specifically for Bearpaw Mountain; treated as N/A for the typical Aug-Sept scramble ascent since it is climbed after snowmelt

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this scramble route

approach_variants.name: FS-3160 road-end boot path to Church Lake, then the basin rim to the 6,066 ft knoll
approach_variants.notes:
From the FS-3160 road-end parking, reached via Canyon Creek Road (FS-31) then FS-3160, the route follows an unmaintained but heavily used boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail. It climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first stretch is the steepest sustained grade of the day.

Skirt the lake along its east (left) shore; the best flat campsites are on the far side.

Beyond the lake the tread fades into intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches. Keep LEFT — west — up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block. That stretch accounts for most of the remaining 900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 miles one way.

Church Lake is the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow patches persist into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
hazards: An unmaintained boot path with no numbered trail and no maintained tread past the lake
Intermittent cairns through meadows and heather with nothing built to follow
Snow patches into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
A loose scree and dirt descent chute that parties use as a shortcut
Church Lake is the last water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CHURCH LAKE IS THE HANDRAIL AND IT IS UNMISSABLE — 0.6 TO 0.7 MILE UP, 400 FT OF GAIN, AND THE STEEPEST GROUND OF THE DAY IS BEHIND YOU WHEN YOU REACH IT. Everything about this route is oriented from the lake. Skirt it on its EAST, left-hand, shore.

ABOVE THE LAKE THE INSTRUCTION IS ONE WORD: LEFT. Keep left — west — up the basin rim. The tread is intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches and there is nothing built to follow, so the bearing is what you navigate on.

THE 6,066 FT KNOLL IS THE TOP OF THE APPROACH: a broad high point on the ridge separating the Church Lake basin from the summit block, only a few tens of feet lower than the true summit. Arriving somewhere the ground falls away on every side is the confirmation.

FROM THE KNOLL, DROP SLIGHTLY AND TRAVERSE NORTH. The base of the summit block is across a rocky heather bowl to the north. That short descent is the step people skip; a party that keeps climbing straight off the knoll is on the ridge rather than under the block.

THE CLIMBING IS THE LAST 300 FT AND NOTHING BELOW IT. From the base of the block, roughly 300 ft of easy Class 2-3 on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure only in the last stretch, reaches the 6,091 ft summit. If you are scrambling for much more than 300 ft you are on the wrong feature.

DESCENT SHORTCUT WORTH KNOWING, because it changes what you should look for on the way up: many parties come down a scree and dirt chute that cuts straight from the ridge to the lake shore, shortcutting the traverse. It is loose. Noting where it tops out on the way up is what makes it usable on the way down.

climbing_route.label: Summit block from the north bowl
climbing_route.notes: Roughly 300 ft from the base of the block to the 6,091 ft summit on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last stretch. Snow lingers in the summit gullies into July on shaded ground; early season that can mean an axe for this section.

bivy.name: Douglas Fir Campground
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
bivy.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
bivy.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up
